Yaseen, Inspector [name withheld] mistook bearded businessman [name withheld] for him; two police parties surrounded the victims' Maruti Esteem at the Barakhamba Road red light and fired 34 shots, killing two occupants and grievously injuring the third. The CBI exposed the cover-up — no shot was fired from inside the car, the 7.65mm pistol was planted, and the policemen's injuries came from police cross-fire — and the Court held the firing was with common intention to annihilate the occupants, spurred by hopes of reward and promotion, rejecting self-defence, superior-orders, sanction and Section 140 Delhi Police Act pleas. Matters not addressed in the cited judgment text are not recorded here.

record.title: Shri [name withheld] vs CBI
record.summary: The judgment of the Delhi High Court records the following account. Sub-Inspector [name withheld] of PS Jahangir Puri demanded and accepted Rs.5,000 from complainant Ashok Kumar on 12 July 1995 as a reward for official favour in a bank-fraud complaint; the CBI trap the same evening recovered the tainted money from him at the police station with positive hand and pant wash. The Special Judge convicted him in December 2002 under Sections 7 and 13(2) read with 13(1)(d) of the PC Act, 1988 (2 years and 3 years SI with fines, concurrent). The High Court held demand, acceptance, recovery and motive proved, confirmed the conviction and sentence, dismissed the appeal and cancelled bail bonds with surrender directions.

record.title: [name withheld] vs Central Bureau of Investigation
record.summary: The judgment of the Delhi High Court records the following account. ASI [name withheld], investigating officer of FIR No. 304/93, demanded Rs 500 per court hearing from the accused Rakesh Kumar in exchange for weakening the evidence, and accepted the money at Patiala House Courts in a CBI trap on 28 October 1996. The Special Judge convicted him under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) of the PC Act and imposed four years RI per count in September 2001. The Delhi High Court held demand, acceptance and recovery proved beyond reasonable doubt through the complainant, shadow and recovery witnesses and matching tainted notes with positive hand washes. It maintained the conviction, reduced the sentence to two years RI on each count concurrent, dismissed the appeal and ordered the accused taken into custody.

record.title: Neema Goyal vs Union of India; Jaspal Kaur vs Union of India
record.unit: Inter-State Cell, Crime Branch, Delhi Police
record.summary: The Delhi High Court awarded Rs 15,00,000 each to the families of Pradeep Goyal and Jagjit Singh, the two businessmen killed in the Connaught Place fake encounter of 31 March 1997, holding the State's liability to compensate for the callous and wanton killing undoubted. With ten Crime Branch policemen led by ACP Satyavir Singh Rathi already convicted of murder at trial, the Court computed pecuniary dependency with CPI-indexed non-pecuniary compensation, interest and costs. It held that criminal trial, disciplinary action and constitutional-court reparation are three independent facets of accountability, and expressed surprise that Delhi Police rules let convicted murderers remain in service pending appeal.

record.title: [name withheld] vs CBI
record.summary: The judgment of the Delhi High Court records the following account. The Special Judge convicted him under Sections 7 and 13(1)(d) of the PC Act with three years RI per count in February 2003. The Delhi High Court held demand, acceptance and recovery proved by the complainant, shadow witness and trap officer with matching notes and positive phenolphthalein washes, despite hostile independent witnesses. It dismissed the appeal as without merit, cancelled bail and ordered the accused taken into custody forthwith.

The Court held eyewitness testimony and a ballistic match between the bullets in the body and the appellant's service revolver proved the intentional firing of four shots, rejecting the plea that the case fell under Exception 4 to Section 300 IPC for want of sudden fight or heat of passion. It upheld the sentences of life imprisonment with Rs 1,000 fine under Section 302 IPC and three years' rigorous imprisonment with Rs 1,000 fine under Section 27 of the Arms Act, to run concurrently, and ordered the appellant taken into custody. record.summary: The Supreme Court decided the suo motu case on the midnight 4/5 June 2011 police crackdown on Baba Ramdev sleeping supporters at Ramlila Maidan, Delhi, in which lathis, tear-gas shells and brick-batting were used to disperse the gathering, killing Rajbala and injuring many. The Court held the police action showed negligence and abuse of power with unjustifiable and brutal acts, while also finding contributory negligence by the organisers Trust. The Court directed disciplinary action against all erring police personnel irrespective of rank, registration of criminal cases, and ad hoc compensation of Rs 5 lakh to Rajbala kin, Rs 50,000 for grievous injuries and Rs 25,000 for simple injuries, with 25% of death/grievous awards payable by the Trust. record.summary: The judgment of the Delhi High Court records the following account. The Delhi High Court held he had misused his official weapon, fired at a vital organ without reasonable apprehension and fled, and that he deserved no leniency given his nexus with criminals. It affirmed the conviction and sentence, dismissed the appeal and directed him to surrender on 6 February 2014 to serve the remaining sentence.

The court held the chain of circumstances complete and drew the custodial-death burden against the policemen, upholding Sections 302/34 and 342/34 while setting aside only the Section 330/34 count for want of extortion purpose. The Court believed the magistrate-recorded dying declaration naming all three, corroborated by extensive bruises at post-mortem, and rejected the suicide and alibi defences. All three kept life sentences under Section 302 read with Section 34 with Rs 5,000 fine, with two also serving two years under Section 330. The convictions came 35 years after the crime. Relying on the nephew's complaint-FIR corroborated by medical evidence, the Court maintained 10 years RI under Section 304-I read with Section 34 plus one year under Section 342/34 and a Rs 25,000 fine from each convict payable as compensation to the widow (Rs 50,000 total), while acquitting a constable and the CFSL Scientific Officer co-accused and setting aside the Section 218/109 convictions. record.title: [name withheld] v. State of NCT, Delhi
record.summary: The judgment of the Supreme Court of India records the following account. On 28 December 1994 guard constable [name withheld], carrying an SAF carbine at I.P. A Section 304A case was first registered, but after the deceased father complaint the Crime Branch chargesheeted murder, and the trial court and Delhi High Court convicted under Section 302 IPC with life sentence. The family sued the State and the PSI for Rs.5 lakh, alleging unauthorised, negligent firing; the City Civil Court decreed Rs.4,35,000 with 10% interest in 1999, holding the deceased a victim of the PSI's negligent and tortious act. The State appealed, claiming the death was caused by private firing during communal riots. The High Court held the firing was without permission and authority, that no mob or curfew was proved, and that the deceased was shot dead without reason by the negligent, reckless and unauthorised act; it dismissed the appeal with costs, confirmed the decree, and directed deposit of the decretal dues within six months.

record.title: Bikram Mohapatra vs State Of Odisha & Others
record.summary: The judgment of the Orissa High Court records the following account. Bikram Mohapatra, a 63-year-old furniture shop owner, was arrested from his shop near Cuttack Chandi Mandir Chowk on 12 May 2026 by Lalbag Police Station on a purported non-bailable warrant in a 2001 criminal case. Subsequent judicial inquiries by the SDJM Bhubaneswar confirmed that the warrant was a counterfeit forgery bearing a fake court seal, and that Mohapatra had no connection whatsoever to the case. The Orissa High Court found the arrest and detention prima facie illegal in violation of Article 21. The Court awarded Rs. 30,000 interim compensation to the petitioner, recoverable from the police or court officials found responsible upon conclusion of inquiries by the SDJM and DCP Cuttack. record.title: [name withheld] and Others v. State by Superintendent of Police, CID
record.summary: The judgment of the Madras High Court records the following account. Alaker Sekar @ Chandrasekar was brought to Odiansalai police station on 29 December 1993 for interrogation and beaten to death by the station police officers; Assistant Surgeon V. Srinivasan (A11) then issued a false first post-mortem certificate attributing death to cirrhotic haemorrhage. A second post-mortem on 3 January 1994 showed death by shock from multiple blunt injuries. The II Additional Sessions Judge, Puducherry (S.C. No. 11/1995, 24.06.2002) convicted three policemen (A2-A4) under Section 304 Part II read with Section 34 IPC with seven years rigorous imprisonment plus Section 201 convictions, and convicted others including the doctor under Section 201. The High Court dismissed Crl.A. Nos. 995, 996 and 1051 of 2002 by common judgment dated 29 October 2018, upholding the convictions; the Supreme Court on 17 September 2025 affirmed the A2-A4 convictions while setting aside only the A6-A8 Section 201 convictions and reducing the doctors sentence to a fine. Matters not addressed in the cited judgment text are not recorded here.

The Court held a policeman swearing a false return to a habeas corpus petition is liable for false evidence, rejecting pleas that he was not bound to file it. The modified sentence of three months' simple imprisonment plus Rs.50 fine was sustained. Matters not addressed in the cited judgment text are not recorded here.

record.title: Roshan Lal and Others v. State of Punjab
record.summary: The Supreme Court affirmed the Punjab High Court's reversal of the trial acquittal of three Jaito policemen for the custodial death of opium suspect Raja Ram. Arrested on 24 December 1961, Raja Ram was beaten at his house and again overnight in the police station to extort a confession, found dead the next morning, and his body burnt with the bones ground and thrown in a canal. The High Court had convicted SHO Roshan Lal under Sections 330, 330/34 and 348 IPC and all three under Section 201 IPC with consecutive three-year terms. With special leave confined to the Section 201 term, the Supreme Court reduced it to one year and nine months' rigorous imprisonment and affirmed the judgment in all other respects. The court rejected the police encounter story, accepting the Sub-Collector's inquest and the Board of Revenue Member's findings that policemen brutally beat Seeralan after capture, concealed facts, filed a false complaint and burnt the body. Holding policemen alone responsible for the death and the criminal acquittal no bar, the court directed the State to pay Rs.1,00,000, retained and invested so as to yield the petitioner not less than Rs.1,000 per month for life. Matters not addressed in the cited judgment text are not recorded here.

The Supreme Court held that the guard's acquittal did not exonerate the appellant since intent at the time of the false entry governed, and that section 42 of the Police Act barred only Police Act prosecutions. It dismissed the appeal, warning that manipulated police records would end honest investigation. In retaliation, Station House Officer Ram Sagar Yadav dispatched two constables to arrest Brijlal on a trumped-up dacoity charge on 29 August 1969, where he was mercilessly beaten inside Hussainganj Police Station. When brought in a collapsed state to the Additional District Magistrate for remand, Brijlal made a dying declaration naming the Darogah and constables before succumbing to nineteen injuries later that evening. The Sessions Judge convicted the SHO and three constables under Section 304 Part II IPC (and the SHO under Section 220 IPC), but the Allahabad High Court acquitted them. The Supreme Court reversed the High Court acquittal and affirmed the convictions and sentences, holding the dying declaration unimpeachable and famously recommending that the legislature amend the law on the burden of proof in custodial violence cases. The Supreme Court dismissed the Moharrir's appeal and allowed the State's appeal, restoring the Sub-Inspector's conviction and sentence on all counts and directing his surrender, famously observing that death in police custody must be curbed with a heavy hand.

record.title: State of U.P. v. K.P. Singh & Ors.
record.summary: The judgment of the Allahabad High Court records the following account. Deshraj Singh was picked up from his field on 5 September 1994 by Station House Officer [name withheld]'s party and detained in the Kunwargaon police lock-up for nearly a week without being challaned in any case, during which he was regularly beaten. record.title: Zulfikar Nasir & Ors. v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
record.summary: The Delhi High Court reversed the 2015 Tis Hazari acquittals and convicted 16 UP Provincial Armed Constabulary personnel of murder and conspiracy for the Hashimpura massacre of 22 May 1987, sentencing each to life imprisonment. The Court found that about 42 Muslim men rounded up at Hashimpura, Meerut, during communal riots were trucked to the Gangnahar canal, shot dead, and their bodies dumped. It termed the massacre a targeted killing of unarmed and defenceless people by the police, relying on survivor testimony and PAC records after the case was transferred to Delhi. Appeals against the convictions are pending before the Supreme Court, which has granted bail to some convicts.

Charge-sheeted only in 1996 with trial transferred to Delhi, all had been acquitted in 2015 for want of identification; on appeal with NHRC-intervenor additional evidence, the High Court held it targeted killing of unarmed defenceless persons. record.title: Ayyappan v. D. Rajagopal & Ors (Ezhukone custodial torture)
record.court: Court of Judicial First Class Magistrate-I, Kottarakkara
record.summary: The Judicial First Class Magistrate-I, Kottarakkara (CC No. 181/1996) convicted Sub-Inspector D. Rajagopal and three constables of Ezhukone police station for dragging complainant Ayyappan from his home to the station on 8 February 1996 over a wage demand against a policeman's kin, and brutally assaulting him in custody overnight — including cigarette burns on his tongue that left him unable to speak when produced before the Magistrate next day — after foisting a false obstruction case on him. The court sentenced each to one year's simple imprisonment plus fines under IPC sections 323 and 324 read with section 34. The Additional District and Sessions Judge (Adhoc)-II, Kollam confirmed the conviction in appeal, and the Kerala High Court (Justice Mary Joseph, Crl.R.P. Nos. 519-520/2013, 23 June 2021) upheld it, holding sanction under section 197 CrPC does not protect custodial torture.
record.trial_court_name: Court of Judicial First Class Magistrate-I, Kottarakkara (CC No. 181/1996)

record.summary: The Enquiry Commissioner and Special Judge (Vigilance), Kottayam, Sri K.V. Rejanish, found former Kerala DGP [name withheld] guilty in a disproportionate-assets case pending for nearly two decades and sentenced him to four years' rigorous imprisonment with a Rs 30.84 lakh fine. record.title: State of Maharashtra v. [name withheld]
record.court: Special Court under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947
record.case_no: Criminal Appeal No.127/1977 (Supreme Court); Bombay HC acquittal 22/23-01-1976
record.summary: Per the Supreme Court judgment of 27-10-1983, Narsingrao Pimple, then a Sub-Inspector attached to Ambarnath Police Station, held up a prohibition charge-sheet against complainant Pandharinath Rege and demanded Rs.2,000 on 09-04-1972 and again on 13-04-1972 to shelve the case, accepting twenty Rs.100 notes in a trap near the Ambarnath octroi naka on 14-04-1972. The trial court convicted him (2 years RI + Rs.2,000 fine) and the Bombay High Court acquitted him in January 1976, but the Supreme Court (Fazal Ali, J.) held the trap proved and the defence a smokescreen, allowing the [name withheld] appeal and convicting him under s.161 IPC and ss.5(1)(a)/5(2) of the 1947 Act with 6 months concurrent RI and Rs.2,000 fine.

The Additional Sessions Judge, Nagpur convicted him u/s 376 IPC (5 years RI + Rs.1,000 fine, acquitting u/s 342); the Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench) set the conviction aside, and the Supreme Court allowed the [name withheld] appeal, restoring the trial-court conviction and sentence.

record.summary: The Special Judge, Pune, in Special Case No.6/1992 on 6 May 1995 convicted Head Constable Sonyabapu Sarjine of Shirur police station for demanding Rs.1,000 at a 26 October 1991 accident spot (paid) to release a brick-kiln truck and then Rs.500 (negotiated to Rs.200) from driver-complainant Dattatray Satav on 20 January 1992 to return seized permit/licence documents, caught in an ACB trap at Shirur police station on 23 January 1992 following the 22 January complaint, sentencing him to 1 year's RI on each PC Act count. record.title: State v. [name withheld] & Ors ([name withheld] custodial death)
record.court: Court of II Additional Sessions Judge, Nagpur
record.summary: In Sessions Case No.416/1993 the Sessions Court on 22 September 1995 convicted all ten Deolapar (Nagpur) police personnel — PI [name withheld], API Yashwant Karade, SI Rambhau Kadu and seven constables — for tying theft suspect Joinus Adam Yellamati to an electric pole and beating him on 23-24 June 1993, after which he was found dead in the lock-up; all were sentenced to 3 years RI under IPC s.330/34 (plus terms under ss.354/355/342) and acquitted of murder. The Bombay High Court (Nagpur Bench) on 13 December 2007 upheld the s.330 conviction of A-1 to A-9 while acquitting A-10 Raghunath Bhakte; the Supreme Court on 4 September 2018 (A-1 having died, appeal abated) upheld the eight convictions and enhanced the s.330 sentence to 7 years RI.

record.title: State vs [name withheld] & Ors (Aniket Khicchi custodial death, Vanrai)
record.court: City Civil and Sessions Court, Greater Bombay
record.summary: The City Civil and Sessions Court, Greater Bombay (Judge Shridhar S.M. Bhosale), in Sessions Case SC 309/2014, on Saturday 30 January 2016 convicted four Vanrai (Goregaon) police constables — Chandrakant Kamble, Kiran Pingle, Umesh Gosavi and one more — for torturing 20-year-old theft suspect Aniket Khicchi to death in custody on the night of 26 October 2013 (56 injuries; post-mortem: head injury with multiple injuries), sentencing each to 7 years RI plus Rs.10,000 fine under IPC ss.304-II and 330; the first custodial-death conviction in Maharashtra, secured after appointment of special PP Rati Amrolia. Convicts' appeals (Crl A. 236/241/250 of 2016) and the victim family's appeals (271/2016, 243/2018) were still pending before the Bombay High Court as of 24 July 2025 (stood over to 25-09-2025).
record.trial_court_name: City Civil and Sessions Court, Greater Bombay (Judge S.M. Bhosale)

record.summary: The Principal Sessions Judge, Cuddalore (Sessions Case No. 99 of 1993, CBCID Crime Nos. 160-162/1992) on 4 September 1997 convicted two sub-inspectors, a head constable and three constables who, as a special theft-detection team, wrongfully confined [name withheld] at Annamalainagar police station from 30 May to 2 June 1992 on suspicion of theft and beat him to death with lathis and boots, while gang-raping his wife [name withheld] inside the station and beating other detained witnesses. The court sentenced the four rapist-constables to 10 years RI each under section 376(2) IPC plus 3-year terms under sections 348, 330 and 354, and the two sub-inspectors to 3 years RI each (sections 218, 323, 348; A-2 also section 220), remarkably without any murder charge being framed. The Madras High Court confirmed the convictions on 28 November 2002 and the Supreme Court (Mehboob Batcha v. [name withheld], 29 March 2011) dismissed the appeal, lamenting that custodial murder by policemen deserved the death penalty.
record.trial_court_name: Principal Sessions Judge, Cuddalore (Sessions Case No. 99 of 1993)

record.title: [name withheld] (private complaint of S. Mallika) v. M. [name withheld]

record.summary: The Principal District and Sessions Judge, Madurai, sitting as the Human Rights Court (CC No. 6/2004), convicted Inspector [name withheld] of Samayanallur police station for illegally detaining S. Anand from 17 April 2003 — shuttling him between Kadupatti and Sholavandan stations without letting his family see him — and brutally beating him with a lathi all over his body, fracturing bones, while also seizing his mother and minor sister at 2 am on 21 April 2003. The court found he violated the victim's fundamental and human rights and sentenced him to a Rs 4,000 fine (Rs 3,500 compensation to the victim) under section 324 IPC read with section 30 of the Human Rights Act, in default one year's RI. The Madras High Court (2 July 2012, S. Anand v. [name withheld]) relied on this conviction while noting the officer had since been promoted [name withheld] despite it.

record.summary: The Additional District and Sessions Judge (Fast Track Court No. III), Vridhachalam, in a common judgment dated 31 May 2004 in SC Nos. 183 of 1995 and 150 of 1997 (CBCID Crime No. 5 of 1994), convicted an SI, two constables and an Inspector of Kammapuram police station for picking up burglary suspect [name withheld] (Kurava community, Mudhanai village) and eight of his relatives between 20 and 22 March 1993, illegally detaining and lathi-beating them in the station — [name withheld] was stripped, tied to a window and beaten black and blue on 22 March 1993 in front of his wife who had brought food — killing him that afternoon, dumping his naked body near Kuruvallappar Koil (passed off as an unidentified 304A death), and fabricating an escape story with a man-missing entry. A-1 and A-2 received life terms for murder. The Madras High Court (Justices R. Balasubramanian and A.C. Arumugaperumal Adityan, Crl.A. Nos. 735, 738 of 2004, 4 December 2006) confirmed the murder, confinement, hurt and evidence convictions of A-1 and A-2 (converting 302/120-B/34 to 302/34 and 324 to 323, sentences maintained), while acquitting A-3 of sections 331/326/354 (convicting him under section 323 with admonition under the Probation of Offenders Act) and dismissing the [name withheld] appeal against A-6's acquittal.

record.summary: The Dharmapuri Principal District and Sessions Court on 29 September 2011 convicted the surviving 215 of 269 officials — including 84 policemen — for the 20 June 1992 Vachathi raid in which a 269-strong forest-police-revenue team ransacked the tribal village, assaulted about 100 villagers and raped 18 women under the pretext of a sandalwood/Veerappan search.
